posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-value ICP prospects (VP Ops, COO, CEO) engaging with a compliance-driven AI ban — validate the auditability problem and add the 'explainability is the real feature' insight without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' answer is basically the end of the conversation in any regulated environment. It's not even about trust in the AI — it's that there's no audit trail, no logic you can walk back through, no way to stand behind the number. The problem isn't that people used AI. It's that the tool couldn't show its working. Curious whether you'd have kept it if it could?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated by Power BI adoption failure — validate the trust problem specifically, add insight about why dashboards fail at the board level, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The trust gap is the real product nobody builds for. Eighteen months of work and the finance team still won't quote a number unless they can see the Excel behind it — that's not a training problem, that's a credibility problem. In my experience the dashboard failing isn't the issue, it's that nobody ever stress-tested the numbers out loud before a high-stakes moment. What would it have taken for your CFO to feel safe enough to actually use it?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post about dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add a layer about why bloat happens in the first place, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The jump from 10% to 85% usage tells the whole story. Most dashboards get built to answer 'what do we track?' instead of 'what do we actually need to know?' — and those are completely different questions. The hard part isn't cutting to 5 metrics, it's getting a room full of stakeholders to agree which 5. How did you handle the politics of that?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: Innovation Director at a retail brand is watching this thread — validate the 'who owns truth' framing and add the insight that the tooling was never the problem, the missing semantic layer was
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so recognisable. Everyone's building dashboards but nobody sat down first and said 'here's what revenue means in this company, full stop.' Power BI didn't cause the problem — it just made the disagreement impossible to hide anymore. The real question isn't who owns the tool, it's who's allowed to define the terms.

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO framing AI hallucinations as a security risk, with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the reframe, add the specific mechanic that makes it dangerous in analytics contexts
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is exactly right and I don't think enough people in analytics are sitting with it yet. The reason it's a security issue and not just an accuracy one is that hallucinated numbers look identical to real numbers — there's no obvious signal something's wrong, unlike a SQL error or a broken dashboard. User inputs get sanitised, validated, flagged. AI outputs in most tools just... ship. What's your view on where accountability sits when the hallucination makes it all the way into a board deck?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with a post about BI tools failing non-technical users — validate the specific £200k waste pattern, add the real reason it happens, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: That £200k story is painfully common. The dirty secret is most BI tools are sold to someone in IT and built to impress that person — the business user never really factored into the design. So you end up with something technically impressive that nobody outside the data team can actually touch without breaking something. What's the point of self-service if you need a data degree to serve yourself?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a likely ICP company naming a real data governance failure — validate the culture diagnosis, add the layer that culture needs a single source of truth to form around
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, three filter sets, one dataset. That's not a culture problem yet — that's what happens before a culture can even form around the numbers. The CFO moment is brutal but honestly it's the forcing function most teams need. Question is whether the response is 'fix the filters' or 'agree on what the number should mean in the first place.'

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the real adoption problem (nobody knows what to ask) — validate the insight and reframe it as a data literacy problem, not a tooling problem
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number doesn't surprise me at all. Most people don't know what to ask because they don't have a clear mental model of what the data even contains — the tool just makes that gap more visible. Shadow AI is the tell though. When people go off-piste to their phones, they're not avoiding AI, they're avoiding friction. What does your data literacy actually look like before someone even opens Copilot?
